output.title: What subscription sprawl is really hiding
output.body:
Subscription sprawl usually looks like a cost problem. In a small business, it often hides a workflow problem: which tool is still being paid for because someone is doing the work by hand?

A good first pass is boring but useful. List every subscription, what it is actually used for, how often it is touched, and what recurring task would stop if it disappeared. That separates active dependencies from legacy extras. Often the monthly fee is not the main cost; the hidden cost is the owner time wrapped around it.

Then pick one repeatable workflow and make it concrete. For example: emails arrive, data gets copied into a CRM, and another tool is used to chase the next step. If that pattern repeats weekly and has a measurable outcome, it may be worth testing whether a bounded automation is a better fit than keeping the tool. If it is irregular, messy, or tied to medical, legal, high-sensitivity financial, bulk cold-email, scan-heavy OCR-dependent work, or requests that need unsupported compliance or security guarantees, leave it manual.

Bareni is a one-person consulting practice being built to work inside the customer’s environment. Finished code is handed over and customer-named accounts are set up from the start; that is policy and no-lock-in positioning, not a legal warranty. Human approval stays in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

The practical next step is not to automate everything. It is to write down one recurring workflow and ask whether it is worth diagnosing at all.
